knowledge_point.title: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Given a Description of the Radius and Angle

question.:question/problem:
If the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $1,$ and that $P$ makes an angle of ${315}^{∘}$ with the positive $x$-axis, then the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are$\,(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$, where

$$
r=1,\,\theta ={315}^{∘}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡({315}^{∘}) \\  & =1\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡({315}^{∘}) \\  & =1\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).$

question.:question/problem: Given that the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $5,$ and that $P$ makes an angle of $\frac{4\pi }{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis, what are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ where

$$
r=5,\,\theta =\frac{4\pi }{3}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ x & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3}) \\ x & =5(-\frac{1}{2}) \\ x & =-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ y & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3}) \\ y & =5(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ y & =-\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-\frac{5}{2},-\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}).$

question.:question/problem:
If the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $4\sqrt{2},$ and that $P$ makes an angle of $\frac{7\pi }{4}$ with the positive $x$-axis, then the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are$\,(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$, where

$$
r=4\sqrt{2},\,\theta =\frac{7\pi }{4}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(4,-4).$
